title: Python
description: Python semantics, data structures, async, typing, testing and common pitfalls.

cards.question: With `def f(x=[])`, what happens to the default list across calls that omit `x`?
options: A new list is made each call
It is shared and keeps changes
cards.explanation: Defaults are evaluated once, when `def` runs, so every call shares one list. Use `x=None` and create the list inside the function.

cards.question: `a = b = []` creates two separate lists.
cards.explanation: Both names are bound to the same list object, so `a.append(1)` also shows up in `b`. Assignment never copies.

cards.question: Which statement lets a nested function rebind a variable of its enclosing function?
cards.explanation: `nonlocal` binds to the nearest enclosing function scope. `global` targets module scope. Without either, assignment makes a new local.

cards.question: A tuple is immutable, yet a list stored inside it can still be changed.
cards.explanation: The tuple fixes which objects it holds, not their contents. Such a tuple is also unhashable, so it cannot be a dict key.

cards.question: What does the `is` operator compare?
cards.explanation: `is` checks whether two names point to the same object. Use `==` for values; use `is` for singletons like `None`.

cards.question: What is the average time complexity of `x in some_set`?
cards.explanation: Sets are hash tables, so membership tests take constant time on average. That is why converting a list to a set speeds up repeated lookups.

cards.question: What is the average time complexity of `x in some_list`?
cards.explanation: A list membership test scans items one by one. Inside a loop this can turn into accidental O(n^2) work.

cards.question: Iterating over a dict yields keys in the order they were inserted.
cards.explanation: Dicts preserve insertion order as a language guarantee. Re-assigning an existing key keeps its original position.

cards.question: Which type adds and removes items at both ends in O(1)?
cards.explanation: `list.pop(0)` and `insert(0, x)` shift every element, which is O(n). A deque is built for fast appends and pops at either end.

cards.question: A list can be used as a dict key.
cards.explanation: Dict keys must be hashable, and lists are mutable and unhashable, so this raises TypeError. Convert to a tuple first.

cards.question: In default CPython builds, the GIL stops threads from running Python bytecode in parallel.
cards.explanation: Only one thread runs bytecode at a time, though threads still help for I/O, which releases the GIL while waiting.

cards.question: In default CPython, what speeds up CPU-bound pure-Python work across cores?
cards.explanation: Separate processes each have their own interpreter and GIL, so they can use several cores. Threads and asyncio share one GIL.

cards.question: What happens when a coroutine calls `time.sleep(5)` instead of `await asyncio.sleep(5)`?
options: It blocks the whole event loop
cards.explanation: `time.sleep` blocks the thread running the loop, so no other task runs. Use `await asyncio.sleep` or move blocking work to a thread.

cards.question: Calling an `async def` function without `await` runs its body right away.
cards.explanation: The call only creates a coroutine object. Its body runs when awaited or scheduled as a task; otherwise you get a 'never awaited' warning.

cards.question: Which call runs several awaitables concurrently and returns their results in order?
cards.explanation: `gather` schedules the awaitables together and returns a list of results in the order you passed them.

cards.question: Python enforces type hints at runtime and raises an error on a mismatch.
cards.explanation: The interpreter ignores annotations when running code. Static checkers like mypy or pyright catch mismatches before runtime.

cards.question: What does a virtual environment isolate?
cards.explanation: A venv has its own site-packages and interpreter link, so each project can pin its own dependency versions.

cards.question: Which file declares a modern Python package's build system and metadata?
cards.explanation: pyproject.toml holds the [build-system] table and [project] metadata. requirements.txt only lists packages to install.

cards.question: Which type hint means a value is either a `str` or `None`?
cards.explanation: `Optional[str]` means `str | None`. It says nothing about the argument having a default; it only allows None.

cards.question: With `typing.Protocol`, a class can match a type by its methods without inheriting from it.
cards.explanation: Protocols enable structural typing (static duck typing): any class with the required methods satisfies the protocol for type checkers.

cards.question: How does a pytest test receive a fixture's value?
options: Name it as a test parameter
cards.explanation: pytest matches test function parameters to fixture names and injects each fixture's return value.

cards.question: Fixtures defined in `conftest.py` are usable by tests in that directory without importing them.
cards.explanation: pytest discovers conftest.py files automatically and makes their fixtures available to tests in that directory and below.

cards.question: `app.py` does `from db import connect`. To mock it for app code, what do you patch?
cards.explanation: Patch where the name is looked up. `app` holds its own reference to `connect`, so patching `db.connect` would not affect it.

cards.question: What does using `yield` instead of `return` in a pytest fixture enable?
cards.explanation: Code before `yield` is setup; code after it runs once the test finishes, even if it failed, so you can clean up resources.

cards.question: Which pytest feature runs one test function with several sets of inputs?
cards.explanation: `parametrize` generates one test case per input set, each reported separately, so one failing input does not hide the others.

cards.question: `''.join(parts)` is the recommended way to build a large string from many pieces.
cards.explanation: Strings are immutable, so repeated `+=` can copy data again and again. `join` computes the size once and copies each piece once.

cards.question: Which avoids building a full list in memory?
cards.explanation: A generator expression yields items one at a time, so `sum(x * x for x in data)` never holds all results at once.

cards.question: What does `functools.lru_cache` do?
cards.explanation: It stores return values keyed by the call's arguments, which must be hashable, and evicts the least recently used entries when full.

cards.question: `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` evaluates to True.
cards.explanation: Binary floats cannot represent 0.1 exactly, so the sum is 0.30000000000000004. Compare with `math.isclose` or use `Decimal`.

cards.question: Which standard library module shows where a program spends its time?
cards.explanation: cProfile records call counts and time per function. Measure before optimizing; the slow part is often not where you expect.
